body_html:
English idioms in Spanish are a classic translation trap. Say “it’s raining cats and dogs” word for word and you will get confused looks. Spanish has its own idioms for the same ideas, often with completely different images: a piece of cake becomes pan comido (eaten bread), and something that costs an arm and a leg cuesta un ojo de la cara (costs an eye from your face). As a translator, these are some of the phrases I look up least and enjoy most. Here are thirty, with the versions used in Mexico and Spain.

Quick answer
  • Piece of cake: pan comido
  • Cost an arm and a leg: costar un ojo de la cara
  • Kill two birds with one stone: matar dos pájaros de un tiro
  • Never translate idioms word for word; translate the idea.
{{toc}}

Everyday English idioms in Spanish

WordMeaningExample
pan comidoa piece of cakeEl examen fue pan comido. (The exam was a piece of cake.)
costar un ojo de la carato cost an arm and a legEse carro cuesta un ojo de la cara. (That car costs an arm and a leg.)
llover a cántarosto rain cats and dogsEstá lloviendo a cántaros. (It’s pouring.)
matar dos pájaros de un tiroto kill two birds with one stoneAsí matamos dos pájaros de un tiro. (That way we kill two birds with one stone.)
romper el hieloto break the iceContó un chiste para romper el hielo. (He told a joke to break the ice.)
dar en el clavoto hit the nail on the head¡Diste en el clavo! (You hit the nail on the head!)
estar en las nubesto have your head in the cloudsHoy estás en las nubes. (Your head is in the clouds today.)
tomar el peloto pull someone’s leg¿Me estás tomando el pelo? (Are you pulling my leg?)

Secrets, luck and timing

WordMeaningExample
irse de la lenguato spill the beansMi hermano se fue de la lengua. (My brother spilled the beans.)
soltar la sopato spill the beans (Mexico)¡Ya suelta la sopa! (Come on, spill it!)
¡Mucha suerte!break a leg¡Mucha suerte en tu presentación! (Break a leg in your presentation!)
cuando las ranas críen pelowhen pigs flyVa a limpiar su cuarto cuando las ranas críen pelo. (He’ll clean his room when pigs fly.)
muy de vez en cuandoonce in a blue moonLo veo muy de vez en cuando. (I see him once in a blue moon.)
hablando del rey de Romaspeak of the devilHablando del rey de Roma… ahí viene. (Speak of the devil… here he comes.)
a última horaat the last minuteSiempre lo hace a última hora. (She always does it at the last minute.)

In theater circles in Spain, people wish each other ¡Mucha mierda! before a show, the local equivalent of “break a leg”. Outside the theater, it sounds rude, so stick with ¡Mucha suerte!

{{image:2}}

Feelings and character

WordMeaningExample
estar en la lunato be miles away, distractedPerdón, estaba en la luna. (Sorry, I was miles away.)
tener mala lecheto be mean-spirited (Spain)Ese tipo tiene mala leche. (That guy is nasty.)
estar de mala uvato be in a bad mood (Spain)Hoy está de mala uva. (He’s in a bad mood today.)
ser pan de Diosto be a saint, very kindMi abuela es pan de Dios. (My grandma is a saint.)
ponerse las pilasto get your act togetherPonte las pilas con la escuela. (Get your act together at school.)
estar hasta la coronillato be fed upEstoy hasta la coronilla del tráfico. (I’m fed up with the traffic.)
meter la patato put your foot in itMetí la pata con su mamá. (I put my foot in it with her mom.)

Idioms that look the same

A few idioms are almost identical in both languages, which makes them easy wins: romper el hielo (break the ice), jugar con fuego (play with fire), llorar sobre la leche derramada (cry over spilled milk), la gota que colmó el vaso (the last straw, literally the drop that overflowed the glass) and más vale tarde que nunca (better late than never).

Many more are true Spanish proverbs; see {{link:spanish-proverbs|Spanish proverbs}}.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

How to translate an idiom you can’t find

When there is no Spanish equivalent, don’t force one. A translator’s approach:

  1. Find the idea. “Under the weather” means feeling a bit sick.
  2. Say the idea simply. No me siento muy bien.
  3. Add color only if you know a local idiom. In Spain, estoy pachucho works well; in Mexico, ando medio malito.

This is the same principle behind {{link:english-words-that-dont-translate-to-spanish|English words that don’t translate to Spanish}}: translate the situation, not the words. The Instituto Cervantes’ Centro Virtual Cervantes is useful for checking whether an expression exists in standard Spanish.

Common mistakes

  • Está lloviendo gatos y perros. Nobody says this. Use está lloviendo a cántaros or está diluviando.
  • Es un pedazo de pastel. It means a literal piece of cake. Use es pan comido.
  • Rompe una pierna. This wishes someone an actual broken leg. Say ¡mucha suerte!
  • Derramar los frijoles. Use irse de la lengua or, in Mexico, soltar la sopa.
{{image:3}} {{quiz}}

Final thoughts

English idioms in Spanish are a lesson in thinking like a translator: find the idea, then find the image Spanish speakers use for it. Learn the thirty above and your Spanish will instantly sound less textbook. For more expressions by country, see my guide to {{link:spanish-slang|Spanish slang}}.

faq.q: How do you say “piece of cake” in Spanish?
faq.a: Es pan comido. In Spain you will also hear está chupado.

faq.q: How do you say “break a leg” in Spanish?
faq.a: Say ¡Mucha suerte! In Spanish theater, performers say ¡Mucha mierda!, but it sounds rude elsewhere.

faq.q: Can I translate English idioms literally into Spanish?
faq.a: Almost never. Look for the Spanish equivalent or explain the idea simply.

faq.q: Are idioms the same in Mexico and Spain?
faq.a: Many are shared, but some are regional, such as soltar la sopa in Mexico or estar de mala uva in Spain.
